newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: FOCUS-Czech GDP growth surprises but clouds loom.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Czech GDP growth surprises but clouds loom.

text.p: The troubled Czech economy showed better than expected first quarter growth, but analysts called for caution even though they had forecast little growth if any at all.
The Czech Statistical Bureau (CSU) released figures on Thursday showing that real gross domestic product (GDP) rose 1.5 percent year-on-year in the first three months of the year.
They also showed strong household demand despite flat retail sales and a sharp rise in inventories.

Analysts in a Reuter poll had forecast growth would be between zero and 0.5 percent. This was based on earlier data showing a contraction in retail sales plus a fall in industrial and construction output in the quarter, and a lack of investment over the period.
"If you look at the drivers of the (GDP) increase it's mainly household consumption," Radek Vavra of Citibank said after Thursday's figures were released.
"(But) in all three months of the first quarter the retail sales have been reported as flat. I'm not sure where the household consumption came from if not from retail sales."
Overall economic output totalled 268.9 billion crowns ($8.4 billion) in the first quarter, up slightly from 264.9 billion for the same period in 1996, when GDP growth was 4.6 percent.

Household consumption remained at the heart of economic growth, the CSU said in a statement. It rose 5.4 percent to about 145.7 billion crowns. Public sector consumption fell 1.1 percent to 62.2 billion crowns.
It also said inventories rose 43.7 percent year-on-year, a statistic that some economists said hid the truth about the economy.

Jiri Krovak, chief economist at WoodCommerz, said GDP would have shrunk more than than one percent in the first quarter if 22.7 billion crowns in adjusted inventories were excluded. This figure compared with 15.8 billion crowns in 1996,
Krovak said he had cut his full-year GDP forecast to two percent growth from four percent.

Other analysts dampened any optimism that the economy was recovering. High interest rates imposed to keep the crown stable during a recent speculative attack would hit the economy in the second and third quarters.
"The effect of rates has yet to be seen. They are going to really choke growth, especially if they last much longer," said one Frankfurt-based economist.

At the end of May a crown crisis caused by a wave of short-selling forced the central bank to raise its discount rate to 13 percent from 10.5 percent and the Lombard rate to 50 percent from 14 percent.

The Czech National Bank (CNB) also cut off access to the Lombard lending facility and agreed with some local banks to keep non-residents out of the local money market to limit the availability of crowns.

It has removed the Lombard and money market restrictions recently, but has not touched its key rates. CNB officials have said the top priority remains crown stability, even at the cost of short-term economic growth.
None the less, the crown reacted positively to the GDP data, firming to 18.545 against the mark from 18.646 before figures were released.

"I expect some small appreciation of the Czech crown but nothing dramatic...It's a surprise because personally we expected (GDP growth) between zero and one percent," said Tomas Becvar, a trader at Komercni Banka.
The economy was given a further dose of positive news by the release of key M2 money figures. M2 growth continued to fall in April to 5.3 percent year-on-year from 6.3 percent the previous month.
The CNB figures include the influence of domestic deposits connected with the $1.32 billion equity expansion of SPT Telecom a.s. in the summer of 1995.
-- Prague Newsroom, 420-2-2423-0003 ($ = 32.05 Czech Crowns)
